analysis.one_liner: Bans credit card interest charges on balances customers pay off on time.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Carl Levin with two Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some credit card issuers charge interest on purchases even when a customer pays the full balance by the due date, because of how interest accrues on charges made during the billing cycle. This bill would change federal lending law to make that illegal: if you pay an amount on time and owe nothing else on the card, the issuer could not add a finance charge to it. The bill never advanced past its first referral to a Senate committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders who pay their balances in full and on time. They would stop paying interest on purchases they already paid for — sometimes called 'trailing interest,' which can appear on a bill even after a customer believes they owed nothing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cardholders who pay in full monthly

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Truth in Lending Act so that no finance or interest charge may be imposed on any amount of new credit that was paid on or before its due date, when no other balance is owed on the account.
Targets the practice where a customer pays the full statement balance by the deadline but is still charged interest on purchases made and paid within the same cycle.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, who would lose the interest income they collect on balances that customers paid on time. If issuers made up that revenue elsewhere, it could come through fees or rates paid by cardholders generally — the bill does not address that.

drawbacks.text: The bill addresses only one charge — interest on on-time payments of a fully paid balance. It does nothing about late fees, penalty rates, or other credit card costs, so it is a narrow fix rather than broader credit card reform.

Card issuers argued generally that restrictions on interest and fees lead them to raise rates or fees for other customers, or tighten credit, meaning some of the lost revenue could be shifted to cardholders who carry balances.

Consumers who already avoid finance charges by paying in full would see little change, since the practice mostly affects people who pay in full but carry a balance from one cycle's purchases into the next month's bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, well-targeted consumer protection: it stops a charge that surprises people who believe they paid everything they owed. The cost falls on issuers, and possibly indirectly on other cardholders if issuers adjust rates or fees. Its main weakness is how narrow it is — it leaves the rest of credit card pricing untouched. Given that it never received a hearing or vote, the practical weighing matters less than the fact that it died quietly in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate read the bill and sent it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Sen. Carl Levin introduced the bill on March 15, 2001, joined by original cosponsors Sens. Dianne Feinstein and Joseph Biden.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired at the end of the 107th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, who kept collecting interest on balances customers paid on time, unchanged by law.

for.name: Sen. Carl Levin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit finance charges on balances paid on time.

for.name: Sens. Dianne Feinstein and Joseph Biden

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote in committee or on the floor, so no party split on the merits can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have banned interest charges on amounts cardholders paid by the due date, cutting off interest revenue from customers who pay in full but get hit with trailing interest. The bill died without action, so issuers' existing practice continued unchanged.
Cardholders who pay their full balance on time would no longer be charged interest on purchases they had already paid for. The savings are real but modest for most households.
